title: Phonetics and Phonology
overview: Speech has a physical form and a patterned organisation. Begin with phonetic description and phonological contrast, then build syllables, word stress and connected speech. Intonation and transcription connect the sound system with meaning in actual interaction.
journey: Describe speech physically: articulation, sound signals and perception.
Identify contrasts and patterns: phonemes, features, vowels and consonants.
Build larger units: syllables, stress, tone and intonation.
Explain an actual utterance: reduction, assimilation, linking and IPA.

topics.title: Phonetics
topics.core: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
topics.explanation: It describes physical speech events, including articulatory movements, acoustic properties and auditory processing.
topics.example: Teaching example: The aspiration after [p] in pin can be measured as a physical feature.
topics.confusion: Phonetics is not restricted to spelling or to sounds that distinguish words.

questions.prompt: Explain phonetics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
questions.answer: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds. It describes physical speech events, including articulatory movements, acoustic properties and auditory processing.
keyPoints: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
Phonetics is not restricted to spelling or to sounds that distinguish words.

questions.prompt: What would an articulatory phonetician examine when you say pin?
questions.shortAnswer: They would examine how the lips close and release, how the vocal folds behave and how the tongue forms the following vowel.

topics.title: Phonology
topics.core: Phonology studies how sounds are organised and patterned in a language.
topics.explanation: It concerns contrasts, distribution, syllable patterns and sound processes. Phonetic evidence helps explain these patterns.
topics.example: Teaching example: English pin and bin contrast through /p/ and /b/.
topics.confusion: Phonology also studies non-contrastive patterns such as allophony.

questions.prompt: What is phonology?
questions.shortAnswer: Phonology studies how sounds are organised and patterned in a language.

questions.prompt: Why is aspiration in English relevant to phonology even when it does not change a word's meaning?
questions.shortAnswer: Its distribution is patterned: voiceless stops are typically aspirated at the start of stressed syllables but not after /s/ in the same onset.
questions.answer: Its distribution is patterned: voiceless stops are typically aspirated at the start of stressed syllables but not after /s/ in the same onset. Phonology explains that organisation.

topics.title: Branches of phonetics
topics.core: The three main branches are articulatory, acoustic and auditory phonetics.
topics.explanation: They study sound production, physical sound signals and sound perception respectively.
topics.example: Teaching example: A spectrogram supports acoustic analysis; tongue position supports articulatory analysis.
topics.confusion: The branches examine related stages of speech rather than unrelated kinds of language.

topics.title: Phone and phoneme
topics.core: A phone is a speech sound; a phoneme is an abstract contrastive unit in a language.
topics.explanation: Phones are conventionally written in brackets and phonemes in slashes. A phoneme can have different phonetic realisations.
topics.example: Teaching example: [pʰ] can realise English /p/ in pin.
topics.confusion: A letter is not a phoneme: spelling and sound units do not correspond one to one.

questions.shortAnswer: /p/ identifies the phonological category; [pʰ] specifies an aspirated phonetic realisation.

topics.title: Minimal pairs
topics.core: A minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound in the same position, with different meanings.
topics.explanation: It provides evidence that the sound difference is contrastive in the language.
topics.example: Teaching example: Pin and bin differ initially in /p/ and /b/.
topics.confusion: Two words differing in several sounds do not form a minimal pair.

questions.prompt: Are ship and sheep evidence for two English vowel phonemes?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Their consonantal frame is the same and the vowel difference distinguishes meaning, supporting a contrast between /ɪ/ and /iː/ in this accent.

topics.title: Allophones
topics.core: Allophones are phonetic variants of a phoneme that do not establish a lexical contrast in the relevant language.
topics.explanation: Their occurrence may depend on context or vary with speaker and style.
topics.example: Teaching example: English /p/ is typically aspirated in pin and unaspirated after /s/ in spin.
topics.confusion: Sounds that are allophones in one language may contrast in another.

questions.prompt: Why are [pʰ] and [p] usually treated as variants of English /p/?
questions.shortAnswer: Their distribution is largely predictable and does not distinguish English words by itself.

topics.title: Complementary distribution
topics.core: Complementary distribution means two sounds occur in non-overlapping environments.
topics.explanation: It supports an allophonic analysis when combined with a plausible phonetic relationship and wider evidence.
topics.example: Teaching example: [pʰ] occurs in stressed syllable-initial pin while unaspirated [p] follows /s/ in spin.
topics.confusion: Non-overlap alone does not prove two phones belong to the same phoneme.

questions.prompt: If two sounds never occur in the same position, must they be allophones?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Complementary distribution needs to be considered with phonetic similarity and the wider sound system; unrelated phonemes may also have non-overlapping distributions.

topics.title: Free variation
topics.core: Free variation is non-contrastive variation in a comparable environment.
topics.explanation: A speaker may produce a final stop with or without an audible release without changing the intended word.
topics.example: Teaching example: Final /t/ may be released or unreleased in a careful comparison of cat tokens.
topics.confusion: Variation can still be influenced by style, social factors or phonetic context.

questions.prompt: Does an unreleased final [t̚] necessarily turn cat into a different word?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. It may be a phonetic variant of /t/ in that environment. The difference in release does not itself create an English lexical contrast.

topics.title: Trubetzkoy and phonological opposition
topics.core: Trubetzkoy helped establish phonology as the study of functional sound oppositions.
topics.explanation: He analysed phonological systems through distinctive contrasts and discussed neutralisation and markedness.
topics.example: Teaching example: A contrast active in one environment may be neutralised elsewhere.
topics.confusion: A sound's phonological role depends on the system, not only its physical properties.

topics.title: Jakobson and distinctive features
topics.core: Jakobson developed analyses of speech sounds using distinctive features.
topics.explanation: Features capture recurring contrasts and natural classes, allowing generalisations across multiple segments.
topics.example: Teaching example: A voicing feature groups contrasts such as /p–b/ and /t–d/.

topics.title: Daniel Jones

topics.title: Generative phonology

topics.title: Diphthongs
topics.core: A diphthong involves a change in vowel quality within one syllabic nucleus.
topics.explanation: Traditional RP descriptions distinguish closing and centring diphthongs.
topics.example: Teaching example: /aɪ/ in my moves from an open quality toward a closer one.
topics.confusion: A diphthong is not identified by the number of written vowel letters.

topics.title: Triphthong sequences
topics.core: Traditional British descriptions call sequences such as /aɪə/ triphthongs.
topics.explanation: They can be analysed as a closing diphthong followed by schwa. Their syllabification and smoothing vary; they are not five extra vowel phonemes added to the usual inventory.

topics.title: Linking and intrusive r
topics.core: In non-rhotic accents, linking /r/ appears before a following vowel where historical or spelling r supports it.
topics.explanation: Intrusive /r/ occurs in comparable vowel-linking contexts without a written r. Both vary across speakers and styles.
topics.example: Teaching example: Far away may have linking [r]; law and order may have intrusive [r].
topics.confusion: These descriptions do not apply identically to rhotic accents.

These descriptions do not apply identically to rhotic accents.

questions.prompt: How do far away and law and order illustrate different r-linking labels?
questions.shortAnswer: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far.
questions.answer: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far. Law and order can contain intrusive r despite no r in law's spelling, in some non-rhotic accents.
keyPoints: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far.
